QUARTERLY ESTIMATED TAX CALENDAR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What do you actually owe the IRS this quarter — and when?

Enter last year's total tax, this year's own estimate (if you have one), and what you've already paid. This applies the IRS's own safe-harbor rule to get a required annual payment, splits it across the four quarters, and shows the real due date for each — adjusted for weekends and federal holidays, not just "the 15th." Then download a calendar file with a reminder before each one.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

Already know your gig-driving net pay and just need to know what to set aside for taxes as you go? See the gig driver net pay calculator's per-session tax reserve — this page is the filing calendar for the quarterly payment itself.

Already have a rough income estimate and just want the safe-harbor floor and the real due dates? See this calendar vs. Keeper's quarterly tax calculator for when each tool is the right one to reach for.

Already tracking this in a spreadsheet? See this calendar vs. a spreadsheet for the three things a formula usually gets wrong quietly — the due date itself, the safe-harbor comparison, and what happens after a missed quarter.

Already missed a due date? See what happens if you miss a quarterly estimated tax payment for how much the next one actually needs to be.

Sell on Etsy, eBay, Poshmark, or another marketplace and already got a Form 1099-K? The 1099-K reconciliation worksheet is the other end of the same tax year — this page sets aside payments as you go, that one reconciles what the marketplace actually reported once the year is over.

Selling a rental or investment property this year instead of just filing on its rental income? The depreciation recapture calculator estimates the tax on the sale itself — this page is for the ongoing quarterly filing, that one is for the one-time sale.

Your numbers

Enter at least last year's total tax or this year's estimate above, then click Calculate.

QuarterDue dateSuggested paymentPaidStill owedStatus

What this does and doesn't do

This computes the IRS safe harbor — the smaller of 90% of this year's estimated tax or 100% (110% if last year's AGI was over $150,000, or $75,000 married filing separately) of last year's tax — and splits it evenly across four quarters, the same default method IRS Form 2210 uses. It does not file anything, does not know your actual final tax bill, and does not model the Annualized Income Installment Method for income that arrived unevenly across the year. Treat every number here as a planning target to verify against the current year's official IRS instructions or a tax professional before paying, never as a filed amount or a determination made on your behalf.

Common questions

How much estimated tax do I actually have to pay each quarter?

The IRS safe harbor is the smaller of 90% of this year's estimated tax or 100% of last year's total tax (110% if last year's adjusted gross income was over $150,000, or $75,000 if married filing separately). Paying that amount avoids an underpayment penalty even if your actual final tax bill is higher. This calculator applies that rule to your own numbers and splits the result evenly across the four quarters.

Are the quarterly due dates always April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15?

Those are the nominal dates, but each one shifts to the next business day when it falls on a weekend or a federal holiday, and the shift can chain through more than one day. Recent real examples: the Q1 2022 deadline moved to April 18 (Emancipation Day observed the 15th, then a weekend), and the Q4 2023 deadline moved to January 16, 2024 because January 15 was Martin Luther King Jr. Day that year. This tool computes the adjusted date for the tax year you enter rather than assuming the 15th.

What if my income is uneven across the year?

This tool splits the annual requirement into four equal quarters, which is the IRS's own default (regular) method under Form 2210. If your income arrives unevenly — a seasonal business, one large late-year payment — the Annualized Income Installment Method (Form 2210 Schedule AI) can lower or eliminate a penalty on the earlier, lower-income quarters. This tool does not compute that method; a tax professional or the IRS instructions for Form 2210 can.

What if I already missed or underpaid an earlier quarter?

This calculator tracks that too, once you enter what you've actually paid per quarter. It compares the total required by each due date that has already passed against the total you've actually paid across every quarter, not just one row at a time. If you're behind, the schedule shows a catch-up amount for the next payment — larger than the flat quarterly share, sized to get back to the safe-harbor pace in one payment. If you paid ahead of schedule instead, the next payment can be smaller, down to zero, and is never shown as negative.

Is this tax advice?

No. It applies a published IRS safe-harbor formula to numbers you already have from your own return, as a planning worksheet — not a filed amount, not a penalty determination, and not a substitute for a tax professional or the current-year IRS instructions.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not tax, legal, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting your actual filing and payment obligations. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage, including an underpayment penalty, arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool except in your own browser's local storage.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (calculate_run, ics_downloaded, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Already missed or underpaid a quarter? The estimated tax penalty calculator estimates the Form 2210 penalty in dollars.

Run a cannabis business? The 280E tax calculator shows why your estimated payments may be far larger than your real profit suggests.

Splitting the year between states? The state residency day counter totals your days per state against the commonly published 183-day tests.

Driving for work? The mileage deduction calculator compares standard mileage with actual vehicle expenses for 2026.

A minister paid partly as a housing allowance? The clergy housing allowance calculator finds the tax-free share and the self-employment tax that still applies.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Quarterly Estimated Tax Calendar

This calendar vs. a spreadsheet

A freelancer, 1099 contractor, or gig worker who pays quarterly estimated tax more than once usually ends up with a spreadsheet for it: a due date typed in for each quarter, and a formula that divides last year's tax (or a guess at this year's) by four. That spreadsheet is correct the day it's built. It fails quietly later — a date that was never business-day-adjusted, a safe-harbor test that only ever checks one of the two IRS branches, or a flat share that keeps repeating after a quarter gets missed — and none of those failures look wrong from the number alone.

What each one is for

A spreadsheet can compute a quarterly tax schedule correctly, and plenty of filers already have one. What it usually doesn't do on its own is shift a nominal due date for the actual weekends and federal holidays of the year you're filing for, run both branches of the IRS's smaller-of safe-harbor test rather than just dividing one number by four, or notice that a missed quarter means the next payment has to be larger than the flat share to catch back up.

This calculator applies IRS Form 1040-ES's own 90%-of-this-year / 100%-or-110%-of-last-year test fresh from the numbers you enter every time, computes the real due date for the tax year you pick (weekend- and federal-holiday-adjusted, not "the 15th"), and tracks what's already due against what's already paid so a missed quarter shows up as a catch-up amount for the next payment, not a repeated flat share.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Can I build a spreadsheet that computes a quarterly safe-harbor schedule? Yes — if the dates are business-day-adjusted for the actual year and the formula runs both branches of the smaller-of test.
Would a formula built around "the 15th" catch a due date that moved? Not unless someone rebuilt it for that year. This calendar recomputes the real date from the year you enter.
Does "last year's tax ÷ 4" apply the 90%-of-this-year test too? Only if the formula does both comparisons and takes the smaller. Most spreadsheets built around one number skip the other branch.
After I miss a quarter, does the sheet tell me the next payment needs to be bigger? Only if someone added that logic. A flat "annual ÷ 4" formula keeps suggesting the same amount regardless of what was actually paid.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere? No. This calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Three things a spreadsheet formula usually gets wrong

The due date itself. The nominal dates — April 15, June 15, September 15, January 15 — shift to the next business day whenever one lands on a weekend or a federal holiday, and the shift can chain through more than one day. Real, published examples: the 2022 Q1 deadline moved to April 18, 2022 (Emancipation Day observed the 15th, then a weekend); the 2023 Q4 deadline moved to January 16, 2024 (the nominal date, January 15, is Martin Luther King Jr. Day that year); and the 2024 Q2 deadline moved to June 17, 2024 (June 15 was a Saturday). A =DATE(year,6,15) formula, or a date typed once and copied down every year, is wrong on all three.

The safe-harbor comparison. Form 1040-ES's floor is the smaller of 90% of this year's estimated tax or 100% (110% above the AGI threshold) of last year's — two numbers, not one. A spreadsheet built around "last year's tax ÷ 4" only ever runs the second branch. On this calculator's own worked example: a filer who owed $15,000 last year and enters that as the only number gets $3,750 a quarter from a last-year-only formula. The same filer entering an $8,000 estimate for this year gets a real required payment of $7,200 for the year — $1,800 a quarter — because the 90%-of-this-year test is lower and wins. The last-year-only spreadsheet ties up an extra $1,950 a quarter — $7,800 for the year — more than the safe harbor actually requires.

What happens after a missed quarter. A flat "annual ÷ 4" formula recomputes the same number every quarter no matter what was actually paid. On this calculator's own worked example: a filer with a $12,000 prior-year safe harbor who has paid nothing by August 1st has a flat quarterly share of $3,000, but two due dates (April and June) have already passed with nothing paid against them — so the amount actually needed to catch back up in one payment is $6,000, twice the flat share a static formula would still be showing.

Open the Quarterly Estimated Tax Calendar to build your own schedule, or see this calendar vs. Keeper's quarterly tax calculator if you're starting from a rough income estimate instead of last year's return.

Common questions

Does a spreadsheet get the quarterly due dates wrong?

Only if it's built from the nominal dates -- April 15, June 15, September 15, January 15 -- rather than the real ones. Each shifts to the next business day when it lands on a weekend or a federal holiday, and the shift can chain through more than one day: the 2022 Q1 deadline moved to April 18 (Emancipation Day observed the 15th, then a weekend), the 2023 Q4 deadline moved to January 16, 2024 (the nominal date is Martin Luther King Jr. Day that year), and the 2024 Q2 deadline moved to June 17, 2024 (June 15 was a Saturday). A =DATE(year,6,15) formula, or a date typed once and reused every year, gets every one of these wrong -- and a reminder set for the wrong day is worse than no reminder, because it reads as on time.

Does a spreadsheet apply the IRS safe-harbor test correctly?

Usually not the full test. Form 1040-ES's safe harbor is the smaller of 90% of this year's estimated tax or 100% of last year's tax (110% above the AGI threshold) -- a comparison, not a single number. A spreadsheet built around 'last year's tax divided by 4' skips the 90%-of-this-year branch entirely, which matters whenever this year's income is lower: on this calculator's own worked example below, a $15,000 prior-year tax bill divided by 4 asks for $3,750 a quarter, while the correct safe harbor -- once an $8,000 current-year estimate is entered -- is $1,800 a quarter, because the 90% test wins and the spreadsheet never ran it.

What does a spreadsheet do after I miss a quarter?

Most keep suggesting the same flat 1/4 share, because that's what the formula computes: annual requirement divided by 4, every quarter, regardless of what actually got paid. This calculator instead compares the running total required by every due date that has already passed against what you've actually paid, and sizes the next payment to catch the shortfall up in one payment rather than carrying it -- and its own interest, under Form 2210 -- to the end of the year.

Is a spreadsheet good enough for a simple year?

For a filer with steady income, no missed quarters, and a AGI comfortably under the high-income threshold, a correctly built spreadsheet using real business-day-shifted dates and the full smaller-of test can get the same answer this calculator does -- the formulas are public, and there's nothing this calculator computes that a careful spreadsheet couldn't. The risk is a formula that goes quietly wrong once: a copied date, a skipped comparison, a missed quarter it never re-checks. This calculator applies the same rules fresh from the numbers you enter each time, so a stale formula can't be the thing that's wrong.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. This calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter -- last year's tax, this year's estimate, or what you've already paid -- is uploaded or stored anywhere but this device.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not tax, legal, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. Verify every figure against the current year's official IRS instructions before relying on it or paying.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any spreadsheet, service, or product — it is a static page describing this calculator's own worked examples.

Free and open source. If it caught a due date you would have missed, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-keeper.html.text:
← Quarterly Estimated Tax Calendar

This calendar vs. Keeper's quarterly tax calculator

Keeper, a bookkeeping and tax-filing app for the self-employed, offers a free quarterly tax calculator that gives a ballpark estimate of what you owe, built from your expected income, business deductions, tax credits, and other taxes for the year. It answers an income-modeling question: starting from what you expect to earn and deduct, roughly what will this quarter's payment be.

That makes it useful for a different moment than this page: estimating a payment before you have solid year-end numbers to work from. This page does not model your income or deductions at all. It takes numbers you already have — last year's total tax, and optionally this year's own estimate — and applies the IRS's own published safe-harbor formula to them, rather than projecting what your year will look like.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Roughly what will I owe this year, starting from expected income and deductions I haven't finalized? Keeper's quarterly tax calculator — it is built to project from expected figures.
What's the exact IRS safe-harbor floor, given last year's tax (and this year's estimate, if I have one)? This calendar — it applies Form 1040-ES's own 90%/100%/110% rule to numbers you already know, no projection involved.
When is each payment actually due this year, not just "the 15th"? This calendar — due dates are shifted for weekends and federal holidays for the tax year you enter.
Can I get a reminder in my own calendar app without installing anything or making an account? This calendar — the download is a standard .ics file with a 7-day-ahead alarm on each unpaid quarter, openable by any calendar app.
Do I want ongoing bookkeeping, deduction-finding, or a tax professional alongside the reminder? Keeper or a similar paid service — this page is a single-purpose calculator and calendar-file generator, not a bookkeeping app.

The two are not substitutes for the full year. A filer who has just started the year with only a rough income guess is better served by an estimator built for that, like Keeper's calculator. A filer who already knows last year's total tax — the number the IRS safe harbor is actually anchored to — gets an exact, published-formula floor from this page instead of a projection, plus the real due dates and a portable reminder that does not depend on keeping an app installed.

This calendar needs no account and no app install: it is a static page, every number is computed in your browser, and the downloaded .ics file keeps working in your calendar app long after you close this tab.

Common questions

Should I use this calendar or Keeper's quarterly tax calculator?

They answer related but different questions. Keeper's quarterly tax calculator (part of Keeper's bookkeeping and tax-filing app for the self-employed) gives a ballpark estimate of what you owe from your expected income, business deductions, and tax credits for the year — useful early in the year, before you have a completed prior-year return to anchor to. This page instead applies the IRS Form 1040-ES safe-harbor rule — the smaller of 90% of this year's estimated tax or 100%/110% of last year's tax — to numbers you already have, shows the four real due dates adjusted for weekends and federal holidays, and lets you download a calendar file with a 7-day reminder on each one. It does not estimate your income or deductions for you the way Keeper's calculator does; it takes the totals you already know and turns them into a payment schedule and due-date reminders.

Does Keeper's app also send quarterly tax reminders?

Keeper's help center describes quarterly reminders and push or text notifications delivered inside its app once you have an account. This page's reminder is a standard .ics calendar file you download once, with no account and no app — it opens in whatever calendar you already use (phone, desktop, work), keeps working if you stop using this site, and does not depend on notifications from a service you have to keep installed.

Is this page affiliated with Keeper?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Keeper Tax Inc. Keeper is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calendar is and is not, based on Keeper's own public description of its quarterly tax calculator and app.

Open the Quarterly Estimated Tax Calendar to build your own safe-harbor schedule and download the reminder file.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not tax, legal, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. Verify every figure against the current year's official IRS instructions before relying on it or paying.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free and experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working.

what-happens-if-i-miss-a-quarterly-estim.text:
← Quarterly Estimated Tax Calendar

What happens if you miss a quarterly estimated tax payment?

The missed quarter's requirement doesn't disappear and it doesn't reset -- it stays open on the running total the IRS safe harbor measures against, until you actually pay it. How much the next payment needs to be depends entirely on how many more due dates pass before you catch up. Worked with this calculator's own example numbers below, and every figure is checked against calc.mjs in this page's test file.

Run this on your own numbers

The worked example

This calculator's own "Load an example" button sets a freelancer who owed $9,500 last year on an $85,000 AGI, with nothing withheld and nothing paid yet. That AGI is under the $150,000 high-income threshold, so the safe harbor is 100% of last year's tax, split evenly across four quarters: $2,375 per quarter. For the 2026 tax year, Q1 is due April 15 and Q2 is due June 15.

Catch it before the next due date, and it costs one quarter's share

Say Q1's April 15 due date passes with nothing paid. If you catch it any time before Q2's June 15 due date arrives, only Q1 is counted as actually due so far -- the running total required is $2,375, nothing has been paid against it, and the one catch-up payment needed is $2,375. That's the same amount Q1 always needed; paying it late instead of on time doesn't add anything to the dollar figure by itself.

Let the next due date pass too, and the one payment doubles

Now say nothing gets paid before Q2's due date passes either. By that point two quarters are counted as due -- a running total of $4,750 -- and still nothing has been paid against it. The single catch-up payment needed to get back on the safe-harbor pace is now $4,750, not $2,375: two quarters' worth in one payment, because the requirement that was already open from Q1 didn't go away when Q2's own share came due -- it stacked.

Point in timeQuarters counted as duePaid so farCatch-up payment needed
Before Q2's due date, Q1 still unpaid1 (Q1 only)$0$2,375
After Q2's due date, both still unpaid2 (Q1 and Q2)$0$4,750

Every additional due date that passes with nothing paid adds another $2,375 -- one full quarter's flat share -- to that single number, for as long as the running total stays unpaid.

Paying "the usual amount" after a miss still leaves you behind

This is the part a flat reminder -- "pay $2,375 every quarter" -- can't catch. Say a filer misses Q1, then simply sends the normal $2,375 for Q2 on time, thinking that settles it. By Q2's due date, $4,750 is required and only $2,375 has been paid: they are still $2,375 short, exactly one quarter's share behind, even though a payment went out and landed on time. What matters is the running total paid against the running total required, not whether the most recent single payment matched the flat quarterly figure.

What this doesn't cover

The catch-up figures above track only the IRS Form 1040-ES safe-harbor dollar amount -- the running total required against what's actually been paid. They are not the full cost of missing a payment: the IRS separately charges interest on an underpayment, computed under Form 2210, and that interest is not calculated on this page or by this calculator. Treat the numbers above as the floor of what catching up costs, not the whole bill.

Common questions

What actually happens if I miss a quarterly estimated tax payment?

Nothing is forgiven and nothing resets. The IRS safe-harbor requirement for that quarter still exists; it just sits unpaid on the running total until you pay it. On this calculator's own worked example -- a filer who owed $9,500 last year on an $85,000 AGI, so a $2,375 flat quarterly share -- missing Q1 entirely leaves a $2,375 gap that stays open until it's paid, whichever quarter you finally send it in.

How much should the next payment be after I miss one?

If you catch it before the next quarter's own due date arrives, the make-up payment is just that one missed quarter's flat share -- $2,375 in this worked example, the same as if you'd paid it on time, just later. It only grows if you let more due dates pass without paying anything.

Does waiting longer to catch up make the required payment bigger?

Yes. Each due date that passes with nothing paid adds another quarter's flat share to the one payment needed to get back on the safe-harbor pace. In the worked example, catching up right after missing Q1 costs $2,375; let Q2's own due date pass too before paying anything, and the single catch-up payment needed is $4,750 -- two quarters' worth, not one -- because the running total the IRS measures against keeps growing every quarter you don't pay.

If I just pay my normal quarterly amount after missing one, am I caught up?

No, and this is the mistake a flat reminder ("pay $2,375 every quarter") doesn't catch. A filer who missed Q1 and then sends the usual $2,375 for Q2 has paid $2,375 total against $4,750 actually required by that point -- still $2,375 behind, exactly one quarter's share short, even though a payment went out on time. The running total, not the single quarter, is what determines whether you're caught up.

Does this calculate the IRS underpayment penalty or interest?

No. This page and the calculator only track the safe-harbor dollar amount required by each due date against what's actually been paid, and size a catch-up payment from that. The IRS charges interest on an underpayment separately, computed under Form 2210, and that interest is not shown here -- the practical effect for a filer is that the catch-up amounts on this page are the floor, not the full cost of waiting.

No warranty. This page is arithmetic on the calculator's own defaults and the published IRS safe-harbor formula, not tax advice. It does not compute Form 2210 underpayment interest. Verify any figure against the current-year IRS instructions or a tax professional before relying on it.
